title: Cross v. United States
lead: A language professor claimed that a summer abroad improved his teaching and justified a tax deduction. The government disputed his primary purpose and the allocation of expenses, so the appellate court required a trial before those questions could be resolved.

actors.name: Ephraim Cross
actors.role: City College language professor seeking a tax refund

actors.name: Mrs. Cross
actors.role: Joint taxpayer who accompanied part of the journey

actors.name: Judge Moore
actors.role: Author of the Second Circuit opinion

proceedings: The district court granted summary judgment to the taxpayers. The Second Circuit reversed and remanded for trial, leaving deductibility and allocation unresolved.
limits: The opinion applies Rule 56 and the tax materials discussed in 1964. It does not hold that any assertion of disbelief defeats summary judgment or that informal language study is nondeductible.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A professor and his family traveled abroad
sections.cue: Trace the itinerary that produced the tax claim.
paragraphs: Ephraim Cross taught French, Spanish, and romance linguistics as an assistant professor at City College in New York. On June 30, 1954, he, his wife, and their dog sailed from New York on a French freighter. During the twenty-one-day voyage to Marseilles, the ship stopped briefly in Portugal, Morocco, Tangiers, Oran, Algiers, Naples, and Genoa. Mrs. Cross then continued touring with a friend while Cross and the dog traveled to Paris. He returned on a French passenger liner and rejoined his wife in the United States on September 23.

Cross took no formal course and conducted no research. He visited schools, courts, churches, publishers, theaters, movies, restaurants, cafés, and other public places; read newspapers, listened to radio, spoke with teachers and students, and attended political meetings. He maintained that exposure to contemporary language and culture preserved and improved his skills and effectiveness as a teacher. Whether that professional purpose primarily motivated this particular trip remained disputed.

sections.title: The taxpayers obtained a refund judgment without trial
sections.cue: Explain what the government wanted to test.
paragraphs: The Crosses claimed a $1,300 deduction for the travel on their joint 1954 return and brought a refund suit. Section 162(a) of the Internal Revenue Code allowed ordinary and necessary business expenses. The regulation discussed in the case permitted educational expenses undertaken primarily to maintain or improve employment skills, with customary professional education relevant to purpose, but generally treated travel as education as personal and nondeductible.

The district court granted the taxpayers summary judgment on a record containing Cross’s discovery deposition and affidavits from professors describing foreign travel’s value for language teachers. It considered the essential facts undisputed, found no governmental evidence rebutting Cross’s purpose, and regarded the opportunity to question him in discovery as sufficient.

The government appealed. It sought to examine Cross and the professors about the claimed educational benefits and expenses, including whether the trip was wholly professional, partly or wholly a vacation, and whether the amount included Mrs. Cross’s expenses. The deposition had been taken for discovery without cross-examination. Its existence did not establish Cross’s subjective purpose as an adjudicated fact.

sections.title: The undisputed itinerary did not settle its purpose
sections.cue: Explain the credibility issue identified on appeal.
paragraphs: Judge Moore wrote for a Second Circuit panel also including Judges Kaufman and Marshall. Under the then-applicable Rule 56(c), summary judgment required no genuine issue of material fact. The trip’s primary purpose, its activities’ connection to teaching, and the allocation of expenses were all material. Knowing that Cross taught languages and traveled abroad did not conclusively establish those ultimate facts.

Much of the relevant information lay within Cross’s knowledge. Competing inferences turned on motive, intention, subjective reactions, and the credibility of his explanation. The government was entitled to test it before the factfinder. The court acknowledged that unsupported allegations in pleadings ordinarily could not defeat a properly supported motion; it did not authorize an opponent to create a trial merely by announcing disbelief. Here, concrete questions about a mixed itinerary depended on the moving witnesses’ credibility. Inability to provide a rival account of Cross’s internal purpose did not make his account conclusive.

sections.title: Educational value still left allocation questions
sections.cue: Keep the possible deduction separate from the full amount claimed.
paragraphs: The court accepted the importance of exposure to current language and culture. Revenue Ruling 64-176 permitted a French teacher’s travel deduction where the itinerary and major activities primarily improved teaching skills. Informal visits, conversations, movies, and plays could qualify; classroom instruction was unnecessary. A trial would give Cross the chance to explain why immersion better maintained his linguistic skills.

But teachers’ educational travel could resemble ordinary recreation. Deductibility required a direct connection to teaching and extended only as far as that connection justified. A lawyer could learn from observing British trials, or a surgeon from a European operation, without deducting an entire summer vacation. The twenty-one-day freighter voyage, Mrs. Cross’s expenses, and charges for the dog illustrated questions hidden inside the aggregate $1,300 claim. The opinion’s joke about a French poodle supplied no independent rule about pet expenses.

sections.title: Both sides would develop the facts at trial
sections.cue: State what reversal did and did not decide.
paragraphs: Relying on Arnstein v. Porter, an earlier decision emphasizing examination and cross-examination before the factfinder, the court rejected treating a discovery deposition as a substitute for calling and examining an adverse party at trial. The district court had improvidently granted summary judgment.

The Second Circuit reversed and remanded for trial, without a separate concurrence or dissent. It neither disallowed the deduction nor declared the whole trip a vacation, and it fixed no deductible percentage. Those factual questions remained open for both sides to develop.
